newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela Oct inflation seen up more than a blip.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela Oct inflation seen up more than a blip.

text.p: Venezuela's October inflation figure, due Friday, is expected to blip up from September's 3.6 percent rate, analysts say.

But that nudge upwards -- combined with a possible recovery in domestic demand -- may signal the need for stronger inflation-fighting efforts by Venezuela's Central Bank, including further export-damaging exchange rate appreciation.

"We have revised our inflation estimate for October to 3.7 pct from 3 percent, mostly as a result of telephone and electricity rate hikes," wrote Caracas-based Santander Investment analysts in a weekly research bulletin.

Government officals have also said they expect October inflation to blip higher following electricity rate rises at the beginning of the month. But while Santander expects "inflation to continue its downward trend", not all economists are so sanguine.

Metroeconomica consultants expect seasonal demand ahead of Christmas and the New Year to keep inflation at around three percent, versus a year-end IMF target of 1.5 to 2.0 percent, and October's figure to even reach four percent.
"The government has not yet reduced public spending," notes Metroeconomica analyst Jose Barcia.

New York-based IDEA also sees signs of inflationary pressure in the money market. Yields on Central Bank six-month TEM bills, which act as a benchmark for wider interest rates, rose at Wednesday's auction.

Although the increase was only a modest two basis points, the rise reversed the pattern of recent months, which "suggests that domestic demand is beginning to recover," IDEA said in a market commentary.
"As such, we expect the authorities to continue to allow modest real exchange rate appreciation to keep inflation on a downward track," IDEA said.
Venezuela's fight against inflation is so far one of Agenda Venezuela's few concrete success stories. Running over the past 12 months at 115 percent, it is seen falling to around 35 percent for 1997.
That victory, however, has come at the expense of an increasingly overvalued bolivar.
Six months after exchange controls were eliminated, the bolivar still trades at around 470 per dollar -- an appreciation that continues to punish a fledgling recovery in non-traditional exports.
"Keep in mind that the exchange rate anchor becomes all the more important as domestic demand recovers," cautioned IDEA.
Although IDEA and Metroeconomica analysts see slow but steady rises in Venezuelan demand, government officials have so far played down growth prospects -- at least for this year.
A healthy return is expected for 1997. But "now is not the right time to start thinking about strong demand growth," Development Minister Freddy Rojas Parra told Reuters in mid- October.

With official unemployment up one percentage point to 11.1 percent over the first six months of the year, President Rafael Caldera recently announced the beginning of Agenda Venezuela 2 -- a more growth-oriented spin on the country's tough IMF-inspired reforms.

And although government officials have said overall growth will return at the end of the year, the economy as a whole is expected to register a 1.1 percent drop in 1996, and the non-oil sector a belt-tightening 3.5 percent fall.
Nevertheless, "we see inflationary expectations beginning to expand," said Metroeconomica's Barcia.
